summary: This paper investigates how language models retrieve bound entities in-context, challenging the prevailing positional mechanism by identifying two additional mechanisms: lexical (retrieval via the bound counterpart token) and reflexive (retrieval via a direct self-referential pointer). The authors design clever interchange-intervention experiments to distinguish all three mechanisms, build a causal mixture model achieving JSS 0.95 against LM behavior, and validate across nine models (2B–72B) and ten tasks. The contribution is meaningful to the mechanistic interpretability community; however, the causal model's evaluation is primarily demonstrated on a single model–task pair in the main text, some statistical reporting is incomplete, and heavy reliance on redacted '[Author] et al.' methodology references makes it difficult to assess how much of the framework is genuinely novel versus inherited from prior group work.
strengths: Novel three-mechanism decomposition (positional, lexical, reflexive) with a causal mixture model that reaches JSS 0.95, clearly outperforming the prevailing one-hot positional baseline (JSS 0.44, below even a uniform distribution).

Clever and rigorous counterfactual design, especially the modified counterfactual (Section 3.4) that distinguishes the reflexive pointer from the answer entity itself, ruling out a suppressive mechanism alternative explanation.

Impressive empirical breadth: nine instruction-tuned models across three families (Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, LLaMA-3.1, 2B–72B), ten binding tasks, and a filler-text generalization experiment connecting mechanistic findings to the 'lost-in-the-middle' phenomenon.

The causal model formulation (Equation 2) is parsimonious and interpretable; the learned σ curve widening at middle indices directly mirrors the experimental observations, providing a tight theory–evidence loop.
Paper is clearly written and logically organized; the running worked example (Ann/Pete/Joe/Tim) effectively anchors abstract formalism throughout.

key_concerns.issue: The causal model M is trained and evaluated on a single model (gemma-2-2b-it) and a single task (music, n=20) in the main text. The claim that M generalizes across nine models and ten tasks rests entirely on Appendix E, which the reader cannot evaluate from the manuscript body. If JSS degrades substantially on larger models or different tasks, the central empirical claim weakens considerably.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Include a summary table or bar chart in the main text reporting JSS scores for M (and the positional-only baseline) across all nine models and at least three tasks; relegate per-model full plots to the appendix. Even a single sentence with mean ± std across models in the main text would help.

key_concerns.issue: Multiple critical method citations appear as '[Author] et al.' due to anonymization (interchange interventions, causal abstraction, the combining-causal-models framework). This obscures how much of the technical machinery was developed by the same group in prior work versus is genuinely new in this submission. Reviewers cannot assess novelty relative to the authors' own prior art.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: This is an anonymization artifact, not a fixable scientific problem, but the paper should more explicitly delineate in the body text which methodological elements are adopted from prior work and which are new contributions of this submission (e.g., the specific counterfactual dataset design, the three-way decomposition, the mixture causal model).

key_concerns.issue: Statistical reporting for the core intervention experiments (Figures 2–4) is incomplete. It is not stated how many samples underlie each bar in Figure 2, whether error bars represent standard error or confidence intervals, or whether differences between mechanisms are statistically significant. The claim that 'the positional mechanism accounts for only 20% of behavior at middle positions' needs uncertainty quantification.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report sample counts and error bars (or CIs) for all proportion plots in Figures 2 and 4, and add a brief significance test (e.g., bootstrap) comparing lexical vs. positional proportions in middle positions.

key_concerns.issue: The reflexive mechanism is introduced as retrieving a target via a 'direct pointer' that only works when the target token precedes the query in context (tentity < qentity), because causal attention cannot look rightward. This architectural constraint is the real reason the reflexive mechanism exists and is necessary, but it is described only informally ('an unintuitive solution, until one considers...'). A more formal statement of when each mechanism is architecturally possible vs. merely empirically dominant would sharpen the claims.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a short paragraph in Section 3.1 or a figure clearly delineating when (i.e., for which tentity values) each mechanism is architecturally feasible vs. merely preferred, and state this as a formal prediction verified by the tentity-stratified results.

key_concerns.issue: The filler-text generalization (Section 5) is evaluated only on gemma-2-2b-it for the boxes task. Given the paper's claim of robustness, at least one larger model should be tested.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add filler-text results for at least one larger model (e.g., gemma-2-9b-it or qwen2.5-7b-it) in the main text or a clearly referenced appendix figure.

questions_for_authors: How does the JSS of the full causal model M vary across the nine tested models? Does the model's near-perfect JSS on gemma-2-2b-it hold for 70B-scale models, where representational capacity is much larger?

The reflexive mechanism is described as retrieving an entity via a direct pointer. Can the authors provide more mechanistic evidence (e.g., specific attention heads responsible, activation patching at head resolution) distinguishing this pointer from a secondary positional look-up? The attention knockout in Appendix F is mentioned but not described in enough detail to evaluate.

The 'mixed' category in the figures captures cases not explained by any of the three mechanisms. What fraction of examples fall into 'mixed' on average, and how does this interact with the causal model's 0.95 JSS (i.e., does the model explain mixed cases via diffuse positional probability or simply assigns low probability to them)?

The counterfactual dataset is constructed so that iP, iL, and iR vary freely from 1 to n. Are there systematic correlations between these indices in real-world text that might render this uniform sampling unrealistic? Have the authors tested whether the learned weights transfer to a naturally-sampled distribution of indices?

Is there evidence that the three mechanisms operate through distinct sets of attention heads and MLP layers, or are they implemented by the same circuitry with different contributions depending on positional context? This would significantly strengthen the mechanistic (as opposed to observational) character of the claims.
calibration_check: Claims are generally well-scoped to the evidence: the paper avoids asserting that three mechanisms are sufficient or exclusive, hedges the 'lost-in-the-middle' connection as a possible mechanistic explanation rather than a proven cause, and the 95% JSS claim is supported by the reported numbers; however, the generalization claim to 'nine models and ten tasks' is overstated in the abstract given that the causal model results are demonstrated in the main text on only one model–task pair.

significance.justification: Understanding how LMs implement entity binding is a foundational question for mechanistic interpretability and long-context reasoning; the three-mechanism decomposition and its connection to 'lost-in-the-middle' failure modes gives the community a concrete, testable framework to build on.

novelty.justification: The positional mechanism was known; the lexical and reflexive mechanisms, their interaction dynamics, and the causal mixture model formalizing their competition are genuinely new, even accounting for uncertainty about what the redacted '[Author] et al.' prior works contributed.

rigor.justification: The counterfactual methodology is sound and well-established; the modified counterfactual design in Section 3.4 to isolate the reflexive pointer is notably rigorous; the main gap is incomplete statistical quantification of the intervention experiment results.

statistical_soundness.justification: CIs are reported only for the causal model JSS scores (< 0.02); error bars and sample sizes are absent from the core intervention proportion figures, and no significance tests compare mechanism proportions across conditions.

calibration_honesty.justification: The paper is honest about the positional mechanism's prior establishment, explicitly notes the confound resolved by Section 3.4, and frames the 'lost-in-the-middle' link as a hypothesis; the abstract slightly overclaims generalization to nine models for the causal model.

clarity.justification: The prose is clear and the running example effective; Section 2's formal notation (binding matrix, template function) is dense but necessary; the mechanism definitions in Section 3.1 are crisp and well-differentiated.

structure_compliance.justification: The paper follows standard conference structure cleanly, with a well-motivated introduction, formal problem setup, experimental sections, and a conclusion that accurately summarizes findings; length appears appropriate for ICLR.

reproducibility.justification: The task templates, intervention procedure, and causal model training setup (70/15/15 split, JSD loss, 150 samples per iP/iL/iR combination) are described sufficiently; however, layer localization details are deferred to Appendix D.2, and the redacted '[Author] et al.' methodology citations leave key algorithmic dependencies underspecified.

related_work.justification: Prior binding and retrieval work (Prakash et al., Dai et al., Feng & Steinhardt, Wu et al.) is thoroughly discussed and honestly characterized; the paper clearly identifies where prior work succeeds and fails; the redacted self-citations limit full assessment of positioning relative to the authors' own prior contributions.

figure_quality.justification: Based on captions, the confusion matrices, layer-by-layer intervention plots, and JSS comparison tables are well-chosen to support the specific claims; the decision to show mechanism proportions stratified by tentity and entity group index is informative and directly ties to the theoretical narrative.

breadth_generality.justification: Nine models across three families and ten tasks is strong for mechanistic interpretability, but the causal model M is validated in the main text on a single model–task pair (gemma-2-2b-it, music), and the filler-text generalization is limited to one model; the claimed generality exceeds what is demonstrated in the main body.

overall_recommendation.justification: A solid, well-executed mechanistic interpretability paper with a clear novel contribution and strong empirical support for the core claims; the main weaknesses—narrow main-text causal model evaluation, incomplete statistical reporting, and obscured prior-work provenance—are addressable in revision and do not undermine the fundamental findings.
